Chapter 7. The Shadow of Empire: Power, Injustice, and the Weight of History.
As time moves on, the world outside the farm gets louder—pressing in with every new law, every tax, and every unfamiliar face showing up at the district office.
The farm owner, who once felt like an outsider herself, now finds she’s standing right in the middle of two very different worlds. She’s trying to honor her own values, but the demands of the colonial system are always close behind, tugging her in another direction.
Sometimes, the unfairness is just impossible to ignore. Imagine this—a Kikuyu family is told they need to leave their land because someone wants to build a new road. The father tries to plead his case, hoping for understanding, but the officials barely listen. Their decisions are made somewhere far away, far from the worries of real people.
The farm owner steps in, wanting to help, but there’s only so much she can do. In the end, the family leaves quietly, holding on to their dignity, but you can feel the loss hanging over everyone who remains.
And then, there’s another day—a Somali herder is accused of stealing by a settler next door. The claim? It’s based on little more than a hunch. But the fallout is very real. The herder is brought before the local magistrate, his future decided by people who barely know his name, let alone his story.
The farm owner speaks up for him, vouching for his honesty and his hard work, but the truth is—no one really knows how it’ll turn out.
These stories shine a light on the deep cracks running through colonial society.
The rules? They aren’t the same for everyone, and the line between justice and power is often blurry at best. Most folks don’t even notice the small injustices that slip quietly into daily life, but on the farm, they build up—leaving scars that take a long time to fade.
But, here’s something beautiful—there are also moments of resistance and quiet solidarity.
When someone is wronged, the farm community pulls together. They share food, offer shelter, and stand up for each other in ways that may not make headlines, but mean everything to those involved.
The owner learns that real leadership isn’t about standing above others—it’s about listening, about learning, and sometimes, about stepping away from the very system she’s a part of.
The shadow of empire stretches long, and its legacy is complicated.
The farm becomes a kind of stage, where all the contradictions of colonial life are played out—beauty and exploitation, connection and division, all tangled together.
And it becomes clear—history isn’t just something you read about in books. It’s written in the lives of ordinary people, in their struggles, and in their hopes for something better.
